{"lessons": ["

Always, often, sometimes

To say how often you do something, Italian has a handful of simple words and phrases.

ItalianEnglish
semprealways
spessooften
di solitousually
qualche voltasometimes
raramenterarely
non... mainever
ogni giorno / tutti i giornieach day / every day
una volta alla settimanaonce a week
due volte al mesetwice a month

Rule: short adverbs (sempre, spesso, mai) go right after the conjugated verb — not before it as in English (\"I often read\").

Leggo spesso il giornale.I often read the newspaper.
Mi alzo sempre alle sette.I always get up at seven.

With a reflexive verb, nothing can slip in between mi and the verb: the adverb comes after (mi alzo sempre).

Longer expressions (di solito, qualche volta, ogni giorno, una volta alla settimana) go at the beginning or the end of the sentence.

Di solito mi sveglio alle sette.I usually wake up at seven.

Two traps. Qualche and ogni are always followed by the singular: qualche volta, ogni giorno. And \"a week\" in \"twice a week\" is alla settimana: due volte alla settimana.

", "

Non... mai, non... più: the double negative

In Italian, the negative has two pieces: non before the verb, and mai (ever) or più (anymore) after it. This double negative isn't sloppy, as it would be in English: it's the correct, required form.

EnglishItalian
I never work on Sundays.Non lavoro mai la domenica.
I don't smoke anymore.Non fumo più.
I never rest.Non mi riposo mai.

Rule: with mai and più, non is required before the verb, and before the pronoun of a reflexive verb.

Non mi alzo mai alle sei.I never get up at six.

The trap for English speakers: \"never\" is a single word, so you're tempted to say \"lavoro mai\". In Italian, that's a mistake. Always say non lavoro mai.

", "

Ancora and già: still, yet, already

\"Always\" and \"still\" are two very different ideas, and Italian uses two different words for them. Don't mix them up.

MeaningEnglishItalian
every timeI always get up at seven.Mi alzo sempre alle sette.
still, right nowDo you still live in Paris?Abiti ancora a Parigi?

Rule: \"still\" is ancora; sempre means \"always, every time\".

Già means \"already\", and non... ancora means \"not yet\". Like sempre and spesso, they go after the verb.

Sono già le otto!It's already eight o'clock!
Luca dorme ancora.Luca is still sleeping.
Non sono ancora pronto.I'm not ready yet.

To answer \"not yet\", two words are enough: Sei pronto? — Non ancora.

title: Always, often, never
topic: adverbs of frequency and their position in the sentence
why: After the routine (reflexive verbs, telling time) and the days of the week, the learner can say what they do; here they learn to say how often, and lock in the double negative non... mai, non... più, with no new verb and at the slow pace they asked for.
